Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no chest X-ray finding answer and a question-specific tool such as chest_xray_expert returns “yes,” or phrase grounding returns the target phrase with a bounding box, but a broad grounded report contains only a related negative such as “no focal lung parenchymal nodule,” or the ROI visual impression seems normal.

Verification action: Before changing the direct positive result to “No,” search the current same-image observations for an explicit negation of the exact object and attribute asked about—e.g., “no mass” or “no mass in the lungs.” Do not treat “no focal nodule,” “no abnormality of the pulmonary vessels,” or a subjective normal-looking ROI impression as equivalent exclusion evidence. If no explicit same-image negation exists, retain the supported positive answer or report the conflict as unresolved. If choices are displayed, map the supported answer text back to the displayed option and confirm its letter and text agree. In this case, chest_xray_expert answered “yes” and xray_phrase_grounding localized “mass” in the right lower lobe; maira2_grounded_report only said “no focal lung parenchymal nodule.” The terminal “No” converted a related negative into an exclusion of mass and contradicted the direct positive evidence, while the released reference was “yes.”

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no chest-radiograph answer to “Are the borders of the heart clearly visualized?”—especially when a report mentions right costophrenic-angle blunting, basal opacity, or normal heart size.

Verification action: Before answering, require a direct same-image observation of the exact attribute: whether the right and left cardiac borders are distinct and traceable, or whether a border is effaced/obscured by adjacent opacity (silhouette sign). Do not treat “heart size is normal,” “blunting of the right CP angle,” or “remainder of lung fields clear” as evidence that the heart borders are obscured; those address different objects/attributes. If a crop was taken, use it specifically to trace the heart borders and do not convert a costophrenic-angle finding into a cardiac-border finding. If the borders can be followed and no observation explicitly states border obscuration, answer “Yes.” If options are displayed, map the supported answer text back to the displayed choice and check that its letter and text agree. If direct evidence conflicts, report the conflict or uncertainty instead of inferring.

Lesson from this case: the grounded report said normal heart size and right CP-angle blunting, but the final “No” inferred right heart-border obscuration from adjacent basal opacity. That was an unsupported leap from a different finding; the reference was “Yes.” A correct grade alone would not prove the procedure was performed—the required check is same-object, same-attribute evidence of cardiac-border visibility.

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no chest-radiograph answer about whether the diaphragm is flat on either side, especially when the draft rationale claims something like “both hemidiaphragms show normal domed contours” but there is no current-image observation or tool result that explicitly addresses bilateral diaphragm contour.

Verification action: Before finalizing, check that at least one observed result from the current case addresses the same object and attribute—the diaphragm/hemidiaphragms and their flatness or contour on the asked side(s). Do not treat historical experience-search cards as current-image evidence, and do not treat a report’s silence about the diaphragm as support for clarity or normal contour. If no such same-object/same-attribute observation exists, do not state the detailed bilateral rationale; either limit the answer to what direct same-question evidence supports or explicitly note the evidence gap. If options are displayed, map the supported answer text back to the displayed choice and confirm the letter and text agree. In the supplied case, “No” matches the reference, but the rationale’s “both hemidiaphragms…” claim was not supported by any listed observation, so the correct grade alone does not validate the final rationale.
